wiki_excerpt:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory of the Caribbean region in the North Atlantic Ocean. It is one of the most northerly of the Leeward Islands in the Lesser Antilles, lying east of Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands and directly north of Saint Martin. The territory consists of the main island of Anguilla, approximately 16 miles (26 kilometres) long by 3 miles (5 km) wide at its widest point, together with a number of much smaller islands and cays with no permanent population. The territory's capital is The Valley. The total land area of the territory is 35 square miles (91 km2), with a population of approximately 15,753 in 2021.


Etymology
The Indigenous Arawakan name for the island was Malliouhana.
In reference to the island's shape, the Italian anguilla, meaning "eel" (in turn, from the Latin diminutive of anguis, "snake") was used as its name. Anguillan tradition holds that Christopher Columbus named the island.


History

Anguilla was first settled by Indigenous American peoples who migrated from South America. The earliest Native American artefacts found on Anguilla have been dated to around 1300 BC; remains of settlements date from AD 600.
There are two known petroglyph sites in Anguilla: Big Spring and Fountain Cavern. The rock ledges of Big Spring contain more than 100 petroglyphs (dating back to AD 600–1200), the majority consisting of three indentations that form faces.
Precisely when Anguilla was first seen by Europeans is uncertain. Some sources claim that Columbus sighted the island during his second voyage in 1493, while others state that the first European explorer was the French Huguenot nobleman and merchant René Goulaine de Laudonnière in 1564. The Dutch West India Company established a fort on the island in 1631, but the Company withdrew after the fort was destroyed by the Spanish in 1633.
Traditional accounts state that Anguilla was first colonised by English settlers from Saint Kitts, beginning in 1650. The settlers focused on planting tobacco and, to a lesser extent, cotton. The French temporarily took over the island in 1666, but returned it to English control in the next year, under the terms of the Treaty of Breda. Major John Scott, who visited in September 1667, wrote of leaving the island "in good condition" and noted that, in July 1668, "200 or 300 people fled thither in time of war". The French attacked again in 1688, 1745 and 1796, causing much destruction but failing to capture the island.
It is likely that the early European settlers brought enslaved Africans with them. Historians confirm that African slaves lived in the region in the early 17th century, with slaves from Senegal living on St Kitts by the mid 17th century. By 1672, a slave depot existed on the island of Nevis, serving the Leeward Islands. While the time of African arrival in Anguilla is difficult to place precisely, archival evidence indicates a substantial African presence of at least 100 enslaved people by 1683. grok_lead: Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory in the eastern Caribbean Sea, consisting of the main island of Anguilla and several smaller islets and cays with a total land area of 91 square kilometres. Located north of Saint Martin and east of Puerto Rico, it has a population of 19,079 as estimated in 2023, predominantly of African descent, with English as the official language. The capital and largest settlement is The Valley. Its economy is small and heavily reliant on luxury tourism, offshore banking, lobster fishing, and remittances, with limited natural resources and unsuitability for large-scale agriculture. Historically administered as part of the Leeward Islands colony, Anguilla was grouped with Saint Kitts and Nevis in 1956 to form the colony of Saint Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla. Resentment over perceived neglect by the Saint Kitts government led to a 1967 referendum where residents voted overwhelmingly for secession, followed by a brief declaration of independence as a republic and a subsequent appeal for direct British administration. After temporary British intervention in 1969 and negotiations, Anguilla returned to full British control in 1971 and was established as a separate dependency in 1980, rejecting full independence to preserve ties with the United Kingdom. This choice reflects a preference for stability under the Crown over regional federation, defining Anguilla's political character as a quiet, low-density territory emphasizing pristine beaches and minimal development.
